o: Three threads must cooperate to emit the exact sequence 0,1,0,2,...,0,n. Each thread can only print its own kind of token: zero() prints 0s, odd() prints odd numbers i = 1,3,..., even() prints even numbers i = 2,4,.... The key observation is that the sequence is fully determined by a single counter i from 1 to n: before printing i we always print 0, so zero() runs n times and even/odd each run floor(n/2) or ceil(n/2) times. This is purely an ordering/synchronization problem — the threads must take turns in a strict cyclic order. Constraints (n <= 1000) mean any correct blocking mechanism is fast enough; correctness of ordering is all that matters.
k: The output is a deterministic function of one shared counter i; every number i is preceded by a 0.
zero() executes exactly n times; even()/odd() execute only when i matches their parity.
Any synchronization primitive that enforces 'only one thread prints at a time, in the right order' works: semaphores, mutex+condition_variable, or busy-wait on an atomic.

a.i: Use three semaphores as permission tokens. A global counter i tracks the next number to print. zero() waits for sZero, prints 0, then signals either sOdd or sEven depending on parity of i+1. Similarly odd/even wait for their semaphore, print i, increment it, then signal sZero. Since each semaphore starts at 0 except sZero, the very first move belongs to zero(), and the chain of signals enforces the exact order 0,i,0,i+1,... with no busy waiting.
s: Initialize i = 1 and semaphores sZero(1), sEven(0), sOdd(0).
zero(): loop n times — acquire sZero, printNumber(0), release sOdd if i is odd else sEven.
odd(): while i <= n — acquire sOdd, printNumber(i), i++, release sZero.
even(): while i <= n — acquire sEven, printNumber(i), i++, release sZero.
Each signal hands control to precisely the thread allowed to print next.
a.t: O(n) total work — each of the 2n printed tokens requires O(1) semaphore operations.
a.sp: O(1) extra space beyond the three semaphores and the counter.

a.i: Keep a single state variable indicating whose turn it is (0, 1, or 2 meaning zero/odd/even). All threads share a mutex and condition variable; each loops until state equals its identity, prints, updates state deterministically, and notifies all. This generalizes easily to any turn order and avoids multiple semaphores, at the cost of notify_all waking all waiters.
s: Initialize state = 0 (zero's turn) and counter i = 1 under a mutex.
zero(): loop n times — wait until state == 0, print 0, set state to 1 if i is odd else 2, notify_all.
odd(): while i <= n — wait until state == 1, print i, i++, state = 0, notify_all.
even(): while i <= n — wait until state == 2, print i, i++, state = 0, notify_all.
Condition variables guarantee no lost wakeups since checks happen under the lock.
a.t: O(n) total work — 2n prints plus O(1) work per turn; notify_all may wake extra threads but total wakeups are bounded by O(n).
a.sp: O(1) extra space — one mutex, one condition variable, a counter and a state flag.

w: In an interview, lead with the semaphore approach — it maps most directly onto the 'who may go next' structure of the problem and is easy to argue correct. The condition-variable version is a good follow-up if asked to generalize to arbitrary turn orders or to avoid multiple primitives. Common pitfalls: forgetting that zero() decides which of even/odd goes next based on parity of i (off-by-one errors here are the #1 bug); using `if` instead of `while` around condition-variable waits (spurious wakeups); letting even/odd spin past n without terminating their loops; and in C++, remembering counting_semaphore needs C++20. Edge cases: n = 1 (only "0" followed by "1", even never prints) and large n (no performance issue at n <= 1000). Likely follow-ups: extend to k threads printing different residues mod k, or eliminate busy-waiting in JavaScript where there are no true OS-level semaphores.
